We have derived mathematical representations of Gaussian random fields that incorporate this bending energy boundary condition in both 2D and 3D dimensions. These representations take the form of specific stochastic equations that reflect the influence of this condition on the curvature of the fields. We have also numerically generated Gaussian random fields that meet these derived criteria for both 2D and 3D scenarios using Monte Carlo methods. Notably, this work has implications for the theory of Gaussian fields and their applications in physics, specifically in the study of phase transitions and statistical mechanics.

We develop a framework for a single view of the $\ell_1$-norm principal component, taking into account rotational invariance, which is essential for classifying data with a non-rotational symmetry property. Leveraging this view, we demonstrate the existence of a unique axis that allows for the distinction of data with a rotational symmetry. Taking a 3D human face as an example, we show that this axis can effectively partition the face into regions of varying importance. Our method employs a novel two-step approach, utilizing non-convex optimization and the $\ell_1$-norm norm, and includes theoretical and experimental evidence of its convergence.

Recently, social media platforms have experienced a surge in annotated text data related to emotions, which has been utilized for various applications such as sentiment analysis, emotional influence analysis, and user behavior prediction. However, the quality of these annotations is often uncertain, posing a significant challenge for models trained on high-quality data. This paper presents a novel approach to revising emotion-related annotations using a BERT-based model. Initially, a team of experts manually annotated a dataset, which was then utilized to train a BERT-based model to predict annotations. This model was subsequently applied to re-examine and revise existing annotations based on their semantic coherence. A BERT-based re-annotation method was also proposed to directly revise annotations by re-annotating uncertain instances. Both approaches were evaluated using three datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed methods in revising annotations.

For mobile robots to effectively navigate complex environments, their spatial representation must accurately capture the layout and enable efficient path planning. This paper introduces a novel navigation framework based on a hierarchical topological map representation, which we call HiTMap. HiTMap combines the global view of a navigation graph with localized, high-resolution slam mappings, allowing it to adapt to dynamic and unknown environments. In contrast to traditional hybrid approaches that maintain separate maps for navigation and localization, HiTMap integrates slam data directly into its navigation graph, via a process called "patching." This integration reduces memory usage and computation required for path planning, while also preventing persistent mapping errors. Our evaluation using a HiGEM simulation and real-world data from the Robot Operating System (ROS) showcases HiTMap's benefits, demonstrating a 2.5 times decrease in memory consumption and a 1.6 times decrease in computation for path planning, without compromising navigation performance.

Our research leverages atomic interferometry to detect magnetic fields associated with the Meissner effect in superconductors. The interplay between the interferometer's non-magnetic nature and the Meissner effect's spatial magnetic field void allows for precise measurement of the associated field strength, which can be as weak as $10^{-5}$ G. This achievement positions atomic interferometry for studying the intricacies of superconducting materials in various settings, including geophysics and quantum physics.

In this work, finite mixture models from (Bühlmann, 1974) and Dirichlet process mixtures serve as our fundamental frameworks. We demonstrate how these models can be represented through a combination of geometric probability and Choquet theory, building on the concepts presented in (Kerber and Mikkelsen, 2011) and (Kerber and Mikkelsen, 2013). We then apply this representation to identify parameters in finite mixture models using an EM algorithm and provide a new algorithm for this purpose. Additionally, we explore the implications of this representation for Dirichlet process mixtures.

Developing high-performance applications on the Single-Program, Multiple-Data (SPMD) model of the GPU using CUDA is a complex task due to memory management difficulties. Although the SPMD model offers significant computational speedup, it creates memory conflicts from concurrent memory access from different threads. This conflict can significantly slow down the GPU's computation power. To address this challenge, a dynamic memory allocator called DynaSOAr has been developed for the CUDA SPMD environment. DynaSOAr efficiently manages memory by allocating memory in small chunks to individual objects, thus minimizing memory fragmentation. Furthermore, DynaSOAr optimizes memory access through the use of 32-byte memory blocks that align with the GPU's memory access alignment requirements. This alignment enables DynaSOAr to maximize memory coalescing in CUDA applications. To facilitate object-oriented programming on the GPU, DynaSOAr provides a virtual table (vtable) that points to the memory location of an object's method. This vtable can be updated using a "set" instruction in atomic form, which is critical for concurrent programming. To demonstrate DynaSOAr's effectiveness, a series of benchmarks have been conducted, including object-oriented programming in CUDA with atomic vtable updates, showing that DynaSOAr achieves a 2 times speedup in computation and a 10 times speedup in memory allocation compared to other state-of-the-art memory allocators.

A theoretical framework based on an initial principles approach has been developed to model and understand the magnetic properties of a single manganese adatom and manganese dimers on a niobium surface. By applying this framework, we simulated and compared the magnetic moments of a manganese adatom in isolation to those found in a superconducting environment, revealing the loss of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states at the Fermi level and a resulting increase in the adatom's magnetic moment from 2.2μB to 3.1μB. Similarly, we investigated manganese dimers and found that their magnetic moments depend on the interatomic interaction, with a separation of 0.2eV leading to a switch from a singlet to a triplet state and a resulting increase in the total magnetic moment from 0 to 4.0μB. These predictions suggest that experimental study of manganese adatoms and dimers on a niobium surface with high-resolution photoemission could provide valuable insights into their magnetic properties.

NASA's TESS has discovered a young star with a remarkable planetary system, TOI-712, located approximately 640 light years from Earth. By conducting a thorough analysis of both light from the star and its planets, TOI-712 system components were identified through detection of three periodic celestial events. A new small dip, likely caused by a fourth planet, was also found. Using data reduction techniques, researchers removed artificial patterns created in laboratory simulations of Earthly conditions from laboratory light interactions with dust particles. This allowed the extraction of precise details about the four planets, revealing they have similar masses and orbital patterns. One of the planets, TOI-712.04, orbits the closest to the star, with a surface temperature between -10 to 10 degrees Celsius, placing it within the habitable zone where water could exist on its surface. TOI-712 is a young star with a low age of approximately 650 million years, and as such, its planets have not had time to stabilize into long-term orbits, suggesting TOI-712.04's orbit may shift significantly.

Rutile titanium dioxide, a significant semiconductor material, has been investigated to enhance its electrical properties while inducing magnetism through the incorporation of carbon and nitrogen impurities. Using density functional theory, we examined isolated impurities in bulk titanium dioxide and found that nitrogen atoms located at the titanium site lead to antiferromagnetic arrangements, whereas carbon atoms in similar positions exhibit no magnetic properties. In contrast, both elements show magnetic properties when situated in the oxygen lattice, albeit with different spin arrangements. Notably, our findings suggest that nitrogen atoms in the oxygen lattice display a rare instance of $p$-orbital mediated long-range magnetic ordering. In addition, we also investigated surface nitrogen and found it induces magnetism at the TiO$_2$ surface.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is expected to operate at 13 TeV for an extended period, providing an opportunity to conduct in-depth studies of top quark production, a key process in the Standard Model. Given the significance of verifying the consistency of the Higgs mechanism, particularly in the electroweak symmetry breaking sector, it is essential to accurately measure the relationship between the top and Higgs boson masses. However, the most basic elastic process involving the top quark, $e^+ e^-$ scattering via a top quark loop, could potentially mask or confuse similar Higgs boson mediated processes. To mitigate this risk, we propose a new search for "exotic" scalar processes that could be misinterpreted as Higgs boson mediated phenomena. This approach involves looking for large forward-rapidity elastic $pp$ scattering at 7 and 8 TeV, with total rapidity gaps of 5 units or more. This search can be performed using existing ATLAS and CMS data. We anticipate that such a measurement could either limit "exotic" scalar processes to the level of 0.02 nb or provide a more precise measurement of this process, which would have significant implications for top quark and Higgs boson mass measurements.

An infinite graph is considered 'rich' if it contains every possible finite subgraph, and 'upper rich' if every of its subgraphs can be formed by a specific, more complex pattern. In this study, we examine the 'upper rich' property of infinite graph components in two-parameter Ramsey theory and establish that only countably many of these components can be 'upper rich'.

We have developed a quantum circuit learning approach for training a qutrit-based gate variational ansatz to simulate the dynamics of a scalar Quantum Electrodynamics (sQED) in 1+1 dimensions. By applying this method to a 1D chain of spinless bosons with contact interactions, we achieved a gate-efficient ansatz for the many-body Schwinger-dyson equation. This resulted in a variational simulation of sQED dynamics using sound waves, represented by the quanta of phonons. Our calculations showed that phonons mimic the behavior of massive scalar fields by inheriting their symmetries and propagating properties. Furthermore, we found that the quasiparticle masses can be significantly enhanced through a "sound enhancement" effect by either increasing the strength of the contact interaction or the speed of sound in the system.

Research indicates that positrons are highly effective at detecting nuclear materials due to their strong interactions with matter. However, as a result of pair production, positrons can also be generated through interactions with intense photons, counteracting their sensitivity. To maintain their detection sensitivity, it is essential to limit positron production to a point where pair production is suppressed. In this study, we examine the pair production suppression condition in the context of interactions between intense lasers and foil targets. Our findings show that even at extremely high intensities, there are optimal target thickness levels where the positron density remains polarized, and pair production is significantly reduced. In particular, we identify a range where the positron density could reach 10% of the electron density in solid materials, reaching densities of 10% with a density of 1015 cm-3 in polarized positrons. This achievement is notable as it surpasses previous records achieved with gas targets by several orders of magnitude. This result highlights the effectiveness and versatility of foil targets in the production of polarized positrons, in addition to their simplicity of design. This research also suggests that the interfaces between the solid surface and vacuum could support unique physics related to QED, which could be further studied under different conditions.

Given a finite nonabelian group G and a subgroup H of G with maximal order, the diameter of G is defined as the minimum number h required for the existence of a chain of subgroups from the identity in H to G itself. Our main findings establish specific constraints on the prime factorization of the order of G for fixed values of h. When h equals 4, we find that the order of G must be divisible by the square of a prime, whereas for h equal to 5, we find that the order of G has a specific prime factorization including at least two prime factors with a particular relationship. These constraints on the order of G can be seen as an extension of a previous result by Shainberg, which focused on h equal to 3.

This research focuses on developing a highly adaptable temperature detection system, capable of functioning across an extremely broad temperature range of -40°C to 150°C, in microscale electronics. A novel approach is proposed to measure temperature using only two bandgap voltages: Vth and Vbg. This method leverages the distinct and predictable relationships between these voltage references and a microcontroller's operating threshold, taking advantage of existing digital resources without requiring additional analog components. The proposed detector's core consists of a 12-bit ΣΔ ADC, configured to convert the combined Vth and Vbg signal into a digital temperature representation. The design of the ΣΔ ADC is optimized for low power consumption and features a 4-bit pseudo-DAC built using a single 6-bit multi-time-programmable memory. The proposed temperature detection system's performance is evaluated through simulations and implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, resulting in a 0.6V to 1.8V operating range, a ±1.4°C error, and a 0.24°C resolution at a power consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion.

This research paper introduces a new concept it terms "geometric frameworks," which applies to both Lie groupoids and higher stacks, and it establishes a direct correspondence between these frameworks and Lie groupoids that are quasi-free.

A long infrared dark filament in the Draco constellation has been observed, and it is proposed that its core may be giving rise to a massive young star. This core, approximately 0.003 solar masses in mass, is located at the brightest end of the filament and is surrounded by a molecular column density of 10 to the 26th bars per square cm. It exhibits a curved shape, with its ends pointing towards the nearby massive young stars NGC 1792-1 and NGC 1792-2. To understand the core's properties and environment, a comprehensive analysis was performed of the core and surrounding gas and dust. This involved creating detailed models of the core's mass distribution and simulating the conditions of the surrounding interstellar gas using plasma dynamics. The results indicate that the core is experiencing compression and is on the verge of collapsing under its own gravity. It is also likely that the nearby young stars are influencing the core with their outflows, which are shaping the curved ends of the filament. Based on observations of the core's motion and the conditions of the surrounding gas, it is estimated that the core will form a massive young star with a mass between 10 to the 2nd and 10 to the 3rd solar masses.

Consider a Gaussian random field defined on the sphere, with a specified covariance function and mean, and assume this field is observed at N equally spaced locations. We aim to provide an one-step recurrence formula to computationally solve the mean squared error minimization for a linear estimator of the unsampled field values. We establish that any linear estimator can be represented through a set of vectors associated with the observed data, and derive the optimal estimator by linking it to the covariance matrix and the observed data vectors. Ultimately, the one-step recurrence formula for the minimum mean squared error is achieved by solving a sequence of linear systems, with a data vector and a matrix associated with the observed and unsampled locations as inputs.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness on the walls of confining channels. This texture can lead to the slowing down and stopping of fluids, even below the critical shear stress required for flow. In this study, we examine the impact of surface roughness on channels filled with liquid foams using computer simulations and compare the resulting friction with experimental data from similar microchannels. Our findings show that liquid foams exhibit higher texture-induced friction compared to other complex liquids, which can be attributed to the unique properties of foams where bubbles interact and share stresses. This interaction causes a sudden increase in texture-induced friction when the stress within the bubbles exceeds a certain threshold, which is directly related to this critical stress. This behavior distinguishes foams from other complex liquids where the texture-induced friction does not exhibit sudden increases. This distinct feature of foams can be explained by a theoretical model that incorporates the distribution of stresses within the bubbles, even in the absence of flow. This model is validated by computer simulations of simple bubble foams. Our research also reveals that the texture-induced friction in liquid foams depends on the surface tension and pressure, which can be influenced by the presence of surfactants. This effect can be minimized by using high-pressure liquid foams, which in turn can lead to the flow of previously stagnant fluids in channels with surface roughness.

A novel approach is presented for detecting and classifying skin carcinomas from dermatological images. This approach involves utilizing a combination of convolutional neural networks to identify carcinoma and a method to detect outlier images, with a subsequent re-training of the network to achieve accurate classification. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through image classification and a proposed dataset, with opportunities for expansion noted.

A droplet of viscous fluid is injected into a rotating cell filled with a more viscous liquid, causing the inner droplet to move in the direction of the cell's rotation while taking the path of a sine function. The occurrence of this specific sine wave-like pattern cannot be predicted by the existing theories for fingering and is influenced by a critical speed below which the pattern described by the Rayleigh-Taylor instability develops instead. A laboratory study of this phenomenon is then carried out and the resulting data compared to the outcomes of two different numerical models, both of which successfully replicate the effects observed in the experiment by incorporating a wavy interface into their simulations.

Astronomers used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to conduct a detailed survey of ethynyl species in the TMC-1 dark cloud. This survey uncovered the ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules CCHCD and CHCCHD at positions 3.823033-0.713937 and 3.822932-0.713937, with line intensities 0.037±0.004 K km s$^{-1}$ and 0.021±0.004 K km s$^{-1}$. These detections, along with previously found signals, provide a first-ever map of the distribution of these molecules and reveal their chemical relationship. The spatial extent of the cyclopentadiene ethynyl molecules is significantly smaller than that of other ethynyl species, suggesting they formed through a different pathway. The abundance of cyclopentadiene relative to ethylene is unusually high in TMC-1, with a ratio of approximately 1.5 times that found in the solar system. This ratio may be influenced by the presence of a specific chemical reaction that also affects the cloud's ethynyl and cyanide compounds.

In neural machine translation, the attention mechanism has significantly improved the accuracy of source sentence representation. However, the effect of attention on target sentence representation remains unclear, particularly with regard to production order. This study proposes a novel look-forward attention mechanism, where the attention weights are calculated based on the generated target tokens in a left-to-right order. We implemented this mechanism in a sequence-to-sequence translation model and evaluated its performance on the WMT14 English-to-German task. The results showed that look-forward attention outperforms conventional attention methods, with an average improvement of 1.05 BLEU scores. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of look-forward attention and found that it produces more coherent and grammatically correct sentences by focusing on the target parts that have been generated rather than those that remain to be generated.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was significantly facilitated by a translational approach that bridged the gap between complex scientific theories and real-world applications. This approach, pioneered by computer scientists Peter Kacsuk, Gergely Születi, and Levente Monostori, transformed abstract concepts into practical tools and helped establish the field of grid computing. By transforming issues of scheduling into manageable algorithms, they demonstrated a key aspect of translational research in action. This experience serves as a valuable lesson for the community of service science research, highlighting the potential for similar breakthroughs through a similar translational method.

The aim of this study is to explore the link between the dark combined fluid model and the Hubble parameter through Pantheon data sets consisting of 289 supernovae, along with other relevant data sets including HST and Cepheid calibrations. By utilizing the Monte Carlo Markov Chain method, key parameters of the model were determined and variations in the model analyzed. The study revealed that the Hubble constant falls within the 3.42 to 3.73 sigma uncertainty range, indicating a discrepancy of this magnitude when compared to standard Hubble parameter estimation methods based on Pantheon data sets.

This study introduces a multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis method for high-dimensional data sets spanning various dimensional spaces, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis and functional time series. It offers an innovative approach to uncovering patterns and reducing dimensionality in data across different dimensional domains, and a computational approach to implementing the method is provided.

This paper investigates the probability that a one-dimensional random walk with zero mean and bounded increments exceeds a certain threshold for an infinitely extended period in a given interval, and we establish that this probability converges to a non-zero limit as the interval's length increases under the assumption of a second moment for the walk's step sizes. Additionally, we provide lower and upper bounds for this probability that converge to the same limit, and these bounds can be expressed in terms of the walk's step distribution and either the length of the interval or the interval's two-sided tail, respectively. This research extends previous results from Snyder (2013) and Dukes and Snyder (2003) by removing the requirement for finite third moments for the walk's step sizes.

The IShTAR plasma generator, a key component for testing ITER plasma protection, operates in helicon mode to create a plasma sheath. To effectively design and test ITER components, it's crucial to understand plasma behavior in this device. This paper presents a detailed analysis of plasma properties based on measurements from three plasma probes placed along the axis of the generator. Results show that plasma properties remain relatively constant across different magnetic configurations, but are significantly affected by power levels. Validation of the device has been completed, with plasma properties matching ITER's required standards in both helicon and RF mode.

Nucleus identification in histopathology images is a critical step for automated cancer diagnosis, but the task is fraught with challenges due to the variability in image staining and the presence of non-nuclear objects such as mitochondria and keratin filaments. To address this issue, researchers have explored the use of automatic nucleus segmentation techniques, but these methods often require significant computational resources and may generate inaccurate results. In this work, a novel W-Net is proposed to enhance nucleus identification by automatically segmenting non-nucleus objects from background. W-Net consists of two stages: a nucleus refinement network and a non-nucleus removal network. In the training phase, the network is presented with unprocessed images, and it learns to refine the nucleus region and remove non-nucleus objects from the background. This is done without access to ground truth nucleus masks. Experimental evaluations on two datasets demonstrate that W-Net can effectively identify nuclei with high accuracy and robustness, and the resulting nucleus masks can serve as input for further analysis such as feature extraction and machine learning-based cancer diagnosis.

Let's consider a prime number p, a finite field F with p elements, its algebraic closure $\overline{F}$, and the absolute Galois group G$_{\overline{F}/F}$. For an odd prime number n, we establish the regional converse theorem for the automorphisms of the algebraic groups $\text{SO}_{2k+1}(Q)$ and $\text{Sp}_{2k+2}(D)$ where Q is a division algebra with a quadratic discriminant and D is a central algebra with a symplectic form. This holds under the condition that the genus of the quadratic form is not split over the prime p and does not lead to a contradiction when combined with the local conjugacy theorems for the tori.

In recent years, Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained significant traction in various applications, surpassing traditional methods in accuracy, yet the underlying principles of GCNNs remain poorly understood. This lack of insight poses a critical challenge for model selection and hyperparameter tuning, as traditional validation methods, which rely on the analysis of models and data, are ineffective. In an attempt to address this issue, we developed a novel methodology based on the analysis of GCNNs as matched filtering systems in signal processing. This framework provides a mathematical framework for the analysis of GCNNs, enabling the application of performance metrics such as mean squared error. By leveraging this framework, we conducted an exhaustive study of GCNNs, including the investigation of spectral GCNNs, spatial GCNNs, and hybrid GCNNs, and a comparative study of various GCNN architectures.

A modified gravity theory, involving a scalar field, can be constructed using a Chern-Simons action in higher-dimensional spacetime. This modification leads to the emergence of a cosmological constant or a negative effective one, depending on the specific dimension. In this context, a scalar field develops a non-zero value in vacuum, resulting in the formation of solitons with specific properties. These solitons can be either stable, with positive energy, and can have a torsion component that affects their rotation rate. When coupled with a Chern-Simons term in five-dimensional spacetime, this modified gravity theory can describe rotating black holes with a scalar hair component. These black holes possess a temperature and an entropy that vary with the scalar field's value, while also exhibiting a phase transition based on their mass and the cosmological constant.

High-resolution elastography imaging is significantly limited due to large lateral displacement estimation errors caused by limited aperture sizes in ultrasound elastography. This paper introduces a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) technique to enhance the precision of lateral displacement estimation in ultrasound elastography. The VOSA approach involves creating a virtual origin at the center of the aperture, with each element serving as a separate transmitter and receiver. This results in a larger virtual aperture than the actual one, leading to improved signal-to-noise ratio and more precise lateral displacement estimation. The proposed method is tested on phantom data and demonstrates improved results compared to conventional methods. When applied to real-time in vivo data with short acquisition times, VOSA exhibits superior performance, outperforming conventional methods by approximately 2.5 times in terms of displacement precision.

High-quality human demonstrations on complex tasks can effectively guide
robots through a learning process known as imitation learning, where a robot
mimics a human performer to master an algorithm it has not been programmed
for. However, when demonstrations are flawed or contradictory, as often occurs
in real-world scenarios, this approach can lead to subpar results and even
safety breaches. To address this limitation, we present a novel concept called
rational pseudocodes, which represents human actions as a hypothetical
algorithm, enabling us to apply popular optimization techniques to correct and
refine demonstrations based on performance metrics and problem-solving
efficiency. When applied to pseudocodes generated from human demonstrations on
SAT solvers and CP solvers, our approach achieves a 2x improvement in solution
finding for SAT instances and a 4x improvement in solution finding for CP
instances, relative to the original demonstrations.

In the context of Euclidean space, the $k$-means clustering algorithm is a fundamental problem that has been extensively studied and optimized for static and dynamic scenarios. This work focuses on the dynamic $k$-means clustering problem, aiming to provide approximate solutions with a guarantee of near-optimal results. We develop a coreset-based approach for this problem, constructing a compact representation that facilitates efficient problem-solving. Specifically, we create a $4(1+\epsilon)$-approximation solution using a coreset of a specific dimension, determined by the original data dimension and precision $\epsilon$. This achievement is significant because it surpasses the previously reported bounds in multiple settings, including both dynamic and static $k$-means clustering problems. Our algorithmic framework involves a two-stage process, leveraging a novel stratified sampling method to enhance coreset construction. We also explore the applicability of our approach to other clustering problems, such as distributed clustering and low-accuracy clustering.

A recent development in multi-agent learning, hierarchical approaches have been applied to complex tasks such as navigation and pursuit-evasion games. In this work, a hierarchical model is applied to a team of agents participating in a stochastic pursuit-evasion competition. Unlike traditional hierarchical models that integrate both low-level and high-level decision-making processes simultaneously, this work separates the agents into two distinct categories based on their roles as pursuers or evaders. Each category employs a different decision-making strategy, with pursuers adopting a greedy approach and evaders utilizing a hierarchical method. Our research demonstrates that hierarchical divisions among agents can significantly improve the performance of a team in pursuit-evasion games by reducing loss rates and improving win rates.

To facilitate precise measurements at future muon colliders, I present a novel, computationally efficient method for determining the properties of vector bosons, such as W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon-proton collisions. This approach, which leverages neural networks, effectively reconstructs the four-momenta of these particles by directly analyzing raw calorimeter data without traditional cluster formation. Neural network training is optimized to prioritize property determination over traditional tasks like jet and lepton identification. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in comparison to conventional strategies, yielding precise estimates of W and Z boson masses, coupling constants, and other key properties with uncertainties as low as 0.1 GeV. This achievement is made possible by the use of advanced calorimeter simulations and neural network architectures, such as the Mixture of Experts approach, which enables efficient computation at a reasonable cost. The efficient vector boson estimation method presented here offers significant benefits for a range of physics measurements at future muon colliders.

In complex environments, reinforcement learning tasks often share similar underlying structures, and many real-world applications involve multiple interconnected components. To address these challenging scenarios, we propose a novel modular approach to model-based multi-task reinforcement learning, where each module represents a distinct sub-component of the state or dynamics. By processing and storing compact representations of their respective dynamics, modules can efficiently handle overlapping information and prevent destructive interference when combining their outputs. This approach ensures that the combined policy and value function maintain consistency across the state space, enabling safe exploration and enabling the system to learn from limited data. Our modular approach outperforms non-modular methods in multiple challenging multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios, including those with latent sub-components and real-world robotics applications.

This note brings together four famous self-improving theories from 1950, 
each preventing a particular kind of contradiction from occurring. 
Wagner (2016) classified five types of self-improving theories, 
and all four of these famous examples exclude the same four types of contradictions. 
Their collective name honors Kurt Godel, Alfred Tarski, Rudolf Carnap, and Alonzo Church, 
whose names are variants. 

A Self-Improving Theory (SIT) is defined as a formal system where if a theorem 
is provably true for all provable theorems, then that theorem is true in reality. 
Four types of contradictions can arise in SITs: 
Löb's paradox, Fitch's bullet, the liar paradox with truth, and the liar paradox 
with validity. 
Each of Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Church avoided one of these four contradictions. 
Their respective contributions are: 
Kurt Godel avoided Löb's paradox by using a system that did not include the concept 
of truth, Alfred Tarski avoided the liar paradox with truth in a system that defined 
truth, Rudolf Carnap avoided Fitch's bullet by using a system with a different 
logical structure, and Alonzo Church avoided the liar paradox with validity in a 
system focused on validity.

This research paper extends an earlier result from harmonic analysis to higher-dimensional spaces. Specifically, we build on a three-sphere theorem for hypergeometric functions, which has been recently established, and use it to prove a three-sphere theorem for eigenfunctions associated with the Dirac operator in higher-dimensional hyperbolic space, SNd+1. This, in turn, provides an alternative proof for a three-sphere theorem in the d-dimensional Euclidean space, Ed. The d-dimensional three-sphere theorem in Ed can also be derived from a three-sphere theorem for a related second-order differential operator, which can be further linked to a Gegenbauer polynomial.

Inverse issues in multi-modal medical images pose a significant analysis challenge due to the presence of missing data. A novel approach is proposed to tackle this problem by employing a conditional GAN, where a regularized CCGAN extracts missing information from medical images with posterior masking. The proposed framework leverages both Wasserstein distance and gradient penalty, resulting in a conditioned conditional GAN that effectively captures complex patterns and generates plausible missing data. The model's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on MRI-CT inverse reconstruction, where the proposed method achieves comparable results with state-of-the-art unpaired image-to-image translation techniques, and showcases promising potential for real-world applications.

This study examines a class of fractional-order dynamical systems with which invariant surfaces do not coexist. It demonstrates that there are specific conditions under which no invariant surfaces can exist for a broad category of fractional-order dynamical systems. It also shows that system stability can be ensured through the disappearance of these invariant surfaces, which occurs if a particular condition is met. This research extends earlier findings related to whole and partial differential equations.

The interstellar medium is dynamic, influenced by the movement of gas and plasma within the galaxy. Pulsar scintillation studies can provide valuable insights into this medium, particularly through analysis of spectral data, which can reveal the velocity and turbulence of the interstellar plasma. By examining the spectra of scintillations from the pulsar B1133+16, researchers have determined its velocity to be 72.6 km/s and its turbulence scale to be 11.4 lambda/delta, although these measurements are subject to change over time. The velocity of this pulsar in its orbit around the galaxy has been calculated as 72.6 km/s, placing it within the mid-range of similar velocities for other pulsars. The findings also suggest the pulsar is located 1.35 kiloparsecs from Earth, and the surrounding interstellar medium may be influenced by a nearby molecular cloud that is moving towards the galaxy's center.

In recent years, neural text-to-speech models have achieved high-quality speech synthesis results, but a significant limitation remains in their ability to generate raw waveform data in an autoregressive manner while handling long-range dependencies. To address this challenge, a new pitch-sensitive and duration-sensitive neural network, called the Quasi-Periodic Dilated Convolution layer, is proposed. This novel layer combines a pitch-sensitive layer and a duration-sensitive layer to capture both short and long-range dependencies in the waveform data. The Quasi-Periodic WaveNet architecture leverages this new layer to generate high-quality speech waveforms in an efficient and autoregressive manner. Experimental results demonstrate that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model achieves a lower 0.76 objective function score than the traditional WaveNet architecture on the LJSpeech dataset. Furthermore, the proposed model yields a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.22, ranking it among the top models in the MOS list.

The bicategorical version of the shadow convention from [arXiv:2209.01667] is established, revealing its equivalence to the combinatorial condition of having two distinct types of associated bicategorical pullbacks.

Researchers investigated how difficult it is to pinpoint sounds originating from a specific ear by playing them through the opposite ear under background noise. They analyzed this challenge in both quiet environments and with additional competing sounds. Studies showed that participants struggled significantly more with identifying sounds in their opposite ear, especially with additional competing sounds. This difficulty was greater when the sounds were played in the right ear than in the left, suggesting a left-hemisphere dominance in sound localization. Furthermore, this difficulty was found to affect low-frequency sounds more intensely.

This paper introduces a novel type of graph neural networks called Lorentzian GNNs, which uses Lorentzian geometry instead of Euclidean geometry in node representations. Leveraging the (1,2)-metric, Lorentzian GNNs incorporate direction and speed information from first-order and second-order neighbor nodes to enhance learning in complex tasks. We demonstrate the benefits of Lorentzian GNNs through classification and link prediction tasks on various datasets, including those with sequential dependencies.

This research tackles a significant challenge in identifying structural parameters based on measurements taken from a structure coupled with a fluid, specifically when the frequency domain data from the fluid is given. A computational method known as the finite element boundary element method is used to model the problem, with the aim of minimizing the difference between calculated fluid pressure and input pressure, with the number of frequency points considered. However, since the number of frequency points exceeds the number of unknowns, a regularization technique is employed to achieve this goal. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through numerical experiments using a sample model with multiple frequency points.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model based on the Tsallis entropy framework, a generalization of Shannon's entropy. This model, which we call the TEDD model, provides a mathematical framework for studying decision-making under uncertainty. Utilizing a single parameter, the Tsallis exponent, the TEDD model offers a versatile tool for examining the complex mechanisms underlying human choice behavior. Our research reveals that the TEDD model can replicate previous findings from the exponential delay discounting literature, and it also detects an inverse relationship between the Tsallis exponent and patience levels in a specific task. Furthermore, the TEDD model reveals distinct subgroups within a larger sample based on the Tsallis exponent, indicating that it can capture individual differences that the traditional model overlooks.

This note delves into harmonic gauge choices that maintain consistency in various gravitational theories, starting with linearized gravity and progressing through its massive extensions, as well as their relationship to the Bichl gauge. Harmonic gauge theories in massive gravity exhibit symmetry that linearizes to a certain gauge fixed version of Fierz-Pauli theory when a specific de Rham complex is used, although this property is lost when another complex is employed. In the context of massive gravity, we outline two distinct harmonic gauge types and highlight their distinguishing features, before transitioning to a discussion on the Bichl gauge and its connection to a specific harmonic gauge that encompasses both of the previously mentioned types.

A new representation of the canonical equilibrium conditions is introduced, utilizing Weyl-Wigner transforms and a phase-space perspective. This representation transforms the Poisson equation into a heat equation, allowing solutions to be determined. The inverse Weyl-Wigner transform then yields the conjugate command in operator form. A direct approach to the solution is also possible, employing a Weyl-Wigner representation and Fourier transformation methods. This framework is particularly beneficial for systems that can be analytically solved in frequency space and are free of odd powers of the field operator. A notable example of such a system is the QED effect known as the "dynamical Casimir force." A solution to the canonical equilibrium conditions is derived for this system using Weyl-Wigner transforms, leading to a determination of its canonical density matrix.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been theoretically applied across various disciplines since its inception. This concept, though initially met with skepticism, has been successfully utilized in both simulations and experiments to achieve desirable outcomes. We have witnessed the incorporation of negative absolute temperature into models and protocols within plasma physics, quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, and even sports strategies. This paper explores the positive aspects of negative absolute temperature and highlights its benefits in specific contexts, presenting a more optimistic perspective on this topic.

We have developed a new "most basic scoto-seesaw" framework that incorporates an inert doublet, a singly charged scalar, and two Majorana-type fermions. This framework offers unique advantages in addressing neutrino oscillation phenomena, dark matter, and the Higgs vacuum stability issue. In the present analysis, we have examined two distinct scenarios for neutrino mass generation and have correspondingly adjusted the relevant parameter constraints accordingly. Furthermore, we have examined both the TeV-scale and the next-to-TeV-scale scenarios for the inert doublet. In the case of the lightest Majorana fermion being the dark matter candidate, we have compared our results with existing literature. We have also investigated the impact of the $Z_2$ symmetry on the neutrino mass matrix, finding that it necessitates a minimal extension of the scalar sector to accommodate massive dark matter. In the context of WIMP dark matter, we have examined the $s$-channel annihilation processes at the TeV-scale, which have been found to yield distinct signatures in the gamma-ray spectra. In addition, we have found that a TeV-scale dark matter mass is compatible with the standard model Higgs vacuum stability, with the additional requirement that the singly charged scalar mass also be in the TeV range.

By adjusting the ratio of $t_{2g}$ to $e_g$ orbital amplitudes, we can mimic the $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing observed in experiments and calculations. A critical mixing ratio is identified where the energy gap between $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ bands reaches a minimum. Below this ratio, the $t_{2g}$ band shifts to higher energies with increasing $e_g$ amplitude, while the $e_g$ band shifts to lower energies. Above this ratio, the $t_{2g}$ band shifts to lower energies with increasing $e_g$ amplitude, while the $e_g$ band shifts to higher energies. We establish the equivalence of the relative quantum topological full subcategory and the relative enhanced topological B-model full subcategory for a class of affine affine affine affine varieties that includes non-singular varieties, defined by equations with coefficients from a field k. These categories are also equivalent for varieties with canonical singularities and certain semi-resolutions in dimensions three and higher.

The accuracy of deep learning models for detecting health issues from chest X-rays can be significantly impaired for patients suffering from certain conditions such as COVID-19, lung cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. This problem is particularly pronounced when these models are applied in a clinical setting where patients with these conditions are being treated and assessed. Researchers have explored various methods to enhance the robustness of these models to such biases but have largely neglected the potential of modifying X-rays to counter this effect. In our work, we experiment with three approaches to artificially introduce biases in chest X-rays and investigate how they impact the models' performance. Our findings show that when image biases are introduced based on Alzheimer's disease diagnosis, the models' performance is negatively affected. To counter this, we explore three methods of modifying X-rays and find that, for Alzheimer's patients, average intensity normalization enhances the models' performance by 3.49% and 4.17% for different models. Our research into modifying X-rays to make them more representative of Alzheimer's patients is the first of its kind and paves the way for further exploration of this innovative strategy in addressing real-world clinical scenarios.

ViDaExpert is a user-friendly application for visualizing high-dimensional vector data in multiple dimensions. It allows users to easily explore high-dimensional data by reducing its dimensionality using a nonlinear t-SNE method. This application provides a range of features for in-depth analysis of high-dimensional data through the creation of a t-SNE map and examination of high-dimensional vectors using a variety of nonlinear techniques. It also includes tools for identifying the most significant dimensions of the data and analyzing high-dimensional data in multiple vector spaces. This paper presents ViDaExpert as a suitable tool for both fundamental and applied research in machine learning, neuroscience, and genetics.
